summary: Describes how Kerberos Version 5 is used with Telnet, defining a suboption of the Telnet authentication option.

eli5.summary: Kerberos is a ticket system for proving who you are. This explains how Telnet can show a Kerberos ticket.

questions: how does telnet kerberos authentication work
subtitle: How a Telnet client and server prove who they are to each other using Kerberos Version 5 tickets.

tldr.problem: Telnet logins needed a way to authenticate with Kerberos Version 5 instead of sending a password, and to get keying material for the Telnet encryption option.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a KERBEROS_V5 authentication type for the Telnet authentication option, with suboption commands that carry Kerberos messages (KRB_AP_REQ, KRB_AP_REP, KRB_CRED) inside Telnet subnegotiation.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard with no recorded replacement. Its main risks are weak random subkey choice and forwarding credentials to an untrustworthy server.

today: RFC 2942 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2941 and RFC 2946.

sections.title: What This RFC Adds to Telnet
sections.content:
RFC 2942 describes how Kerberos Version 5 is used with the Telnet protocol. It defines one authentication suboption that plugs into the Telnet authentication option, which is specified in RFC 2941.

The same mechanism can also supply keying material for data confidentiality, in conjunction with the Telnet encryption option from RFC 2946.
sections.eli5: Telnet already has a place to plug in different ways of proving who you are. This RFC adds the Kerberos ticket way.

sections.title: Type and Command Codes
sections.content:
The authentication type is KERBEROS_V5, with the value 2. Seven suboption commands carry the exchange: AUTH (0), REJECT (1), ACCEPT (2), RESPONSE (3), FORWARD (4), FORWARD_ACCEPT (5) and FORWARD_REJECT (6).

Each command sits inside a Telnet subnegotiation of the form IAC SB AUTHENTICATION ... IAC SE and begins with an authentication-type pair. The first octet of the pair is KERBEROS_V5. The second octet holds flags such as who authenticates to whom and whether authentication is one-way or mutual.
sections.eli5: Each kind of message has a small number, like a secret code word, so both sides know whether it is a request, a yes or a no.

sections.title: What Each Command Does
sections.content:
AUTH passes a Kerberos V5 KRB_AP_REQ message to the other side. Its authenticator must contain a Kerberos V5 checksum of the two-byte authentication type pair, and the receiving server must verify it so that the negotiated type pair is known to be correct. The authenticator must also include the optional subkey field, filled with a randomly chosen key. That key is used for encryption if encryption is negotiated, and serves as the negotiated session key (keyid 0) for the Telnet encryption option. If no subkey is present, the ticket session key is used instead.

If data confidentiality is wanted, the ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT flag must be set in the type pair.

ACCEPT means authentication succeeded. REJECT means it failed, and any extra data is an ASCII text reason. RESPONSE carries a KRB_AP_REP message and is used for mutual authentication, only when the AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL bit is set. In that case RESPONSE must be sent before ACCEPT.

FORWARD sends a KRB_CRED message so that Kerberos credentials can be used by the remote session. It includes the forwarded ticket and its session key, and part of it is encrypted in the key already exchanged by AUTH. The reply is FORWARD_ACCEPT on success or FORWARD_REJECT with optional ASCII reason text.
sections.eli5: One side shows its ticket, the other says yes or no. If both want to be sure of each other, the second side shows its own ticket too. A separate step can hand over your ticket so you can use it on the far computer.

sections.title: Who Goes First and Other Rules
sections.content:
If the AUTH_WHO bit is AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER, the client sends the first AUTH and the server answers with ACCEPT or REJECT. With AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL, the server sends RESPONSE before ACCEPT. If AUTH_WHO is AUTH_SERVER_TO_CLIENT, the roles are swapped.

The server's Kerberos principal is generally of the form host/<hostname>@realm: the first component is host, the second is the fully qualified lower-case hostname, and the realm is the Kerberos realm of the server.

Any Telnet IAC byte inside the KRB_AP_REQ, KRB_AP_REP, KRB_CRED or rejection text must be doubled, as specified in RFC 855. Otherwise the next byte could be mistaken for a Telnet command.
sections.eli5: Whoever is asked to prove themselves goes first. And because one special byte means something to Telnet, it has to be written twice whenever it shows up inside a ticket.

sections.title: A Worked Login
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, user joe wants to log in as user pete on machine foo, and pete has allowed this. The client sends the account name with IAC SB AUTHENTICATION NAME, then an IS KERBEROS_V5 ... AUTH command with the KRB_AP_REQ. The server works out that the user is joe from the Kerberos message and checks that pete permits joe.

In the full sequence, the server first asks for mutual Version 5 Kerberos authentication and says it will accept one-way authentication if mutual is not supported. The client sends the name and ticket, the server sends RESPONSE to prove it is the right server, then ACCEPT. If forwarding was requested, the client sends FORWARD and the server answers FORWARD_ACCEPT or FORWARD_REJECT.
sections.eli5: Joe shows his pass and says he wants to enter as Pete. The building checks the pass, shows its own badge back, and then lets him in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The random subkey is critical, because it encrypts the Telnet data stream when encryption is enabled. The RFC strongly advises choosing it with cryptographic techniques that involve the ticket's session key. Its example is to take the current time, encrypt it with the ticket session key and correct the key parity.

Forwarding credentials to an untrustworthy server could compromise them. User interfaces should not forward by default. They should require an explicit request for each connection, or use a trusted list of hosts.

The NAME message is unprotected, so its contents should be verified by a secure method after authentication completes before it is used.
sections.eli5: Do not hand your pass to a stranger, and pick your secret number in a way nobody can guess. Also double-check the name someone gives, because that part is not locked up.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The KERBEROS_V5 authentication type and its suboption values are registered with IANA. Any new suboption values that extend the protocol must be registered before use, and IANA is instructed not to issue new values without documentation of their use.
sections.eli5: The code numbers are written in an official list, and nobody may add new ones without explaining what they are for.
